etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pursuen, from Anglo-Norman pursure, poursuire etc., from Latin prōsequor (though influenced by persequor). Doublet of prosecute.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To follow urgently, originally with intent to capture or harm; to chase. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 15 September 2009, Martin Chulov, “Iraqi shoe-thrower claims he suffered torture in jail”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: He now feared for his life, and believed US intelligence agents would pursue him.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To follow, travel down (a particular way, course of action etc.). [from late 14th c.]
(transitive) To aim for, go after (a specified objective, situation etc.). [from late 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1 December 2009, Benjamin Pogrund, “Freeze won't hurt Netanyahu”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: He even stands to gain in world terms: his noisy critics strengthen his projected image of a man determined to pursue peace with Palestinians.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To participate in (an activity, business etc.); to practise, follow (a profession). [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 2001, David L. Lieber, Jules Harlow, Etz Hayim: Torah and Commentary, page 141:
quote.text: The Kedarites are depicted as herders of sheep and goats who pursued a seminomadic existence and lived scattered over a wide area of the desert region east of the land of Israel.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act as a legal prosecutor.
(transitive, somewhat archaic) To continue; to carry on.

quote.citation: 1870, Richard Francis Burton, “Conclusion”, in Vikram and the Vampire; or, Tales of Hindu Devilry, London: Longmans, Green, and Co, page 307:
quote.text: 'Allow me, great king,' pursued the Demon, in a dry tone of voice, 'to wish you joy  […]
